resources.string: Step by step, from mate in one to endgames
Twenty-seven short chapters, from mate in one to endgames. Each has ten puzzles, getting a little harder as you go. Work through them in order, or open any chapter.
Solve every puzzle to finish a chapter. Two stars: at least 8 of 10 without a mistake or a hint. Three stars: all of them.
Solved without a mistake or a hint: %1$d of %2$d
This time: %1$d of %2$d on the first try
Look at every check first. One of them ends the game.
Count the squares the king could run to, and find the move that covers them all.
A king behind its own pawns has no way out. A rook or queen on the last rank can mate it.
Smothered, Arabian, Anastasia\'s and other classic mates. Notice how the king\'s own pieces block its escape.
The first move is often a check or a sacrifice that forces the king where you want it.
If no check works, look for a quiet move that takes away the last escape square.
Plan backwards: find the final mate, then the moves that force it.
Before anything else, check what is undefended. Free material is the easiest win.
One piece attacking two things at once. Knights are the best at it; look at every knight jump.
Sometimes a check or a capture first puts the pieces on the right squares for a fork.
A piece in front of its king cannot move. Attack it again, or win what is behind it.
Attack the valuable piece first; when it moves away, take the one behind it.
Move one piece out of the way and the piece behind it attacks. Best when the moving piece threatens too.
A piece with no safe squares can be won. Count its escape squares, then take them away.
Some pieces defend two things. Force them away, or capture them, and something falls.
A sacrifice can pull the king or another piece onto a bad square, often into a fork or mate.
Giving material is fine when what follows wins more: mate, or more material back.
Your own piece can be in the way. Move it with tempo to open a line for another.
Before recapturing, look for a stronger move: a check or a threat the opponent must answer.
Not every winning move is a check or capture. Sometimes a calm move leaves the opponent with nothing good.
Here you are under attack. Find the only move that holds: block, defend, or counter-attack.
A pawn close to the last rank is worth a queen. Clear its path or distract the piece that stops it.
With only pawns left, king position decides. Count moves carefully: one tempo can win or lose.
Rooks belong behind passed pawns. An active rook is often worth a pawn.
Bishops love open boards and pawns on both sides; knights like closed positions and outposts.
Queens give many checks. Find the one that wins material or forces the king into a mate net.
Sometimes the best move is the one that makes the opponent move. Every move they have makes things worse.
Solve puzzles from different themes to see where to practise. A theme shows here after %1$d tries.
The same puzzles again, faster each time
A repeat set is a fixed group of puzzles you solve again and again. Each cycle, try to be a little faster and make fewer mistakes, until the patterns come without thinking.
No puzzles with mistakes yet. Choose Near my level.
Start a new set? The cycles of this one are cleared.
Time counts only while a puzzle is on the board. A good aim is to halve your time over a few cycles.
%1$s does not work here. Try again.
Not rated: only the first try at a puzzle counts.
Your puzzle rating goes up when you solve a puzzle on the first try and down when you need help or give up. Harder puzzles give more points. Each puzzle counts once, the first time you try it.
Rated: this game counts towards your game rating (now %1$s). Taking back a move or using a hint makes it unrated.
Unrated: games with the evaluation on, or from an imported position, don\'t count towards your rating.
This game will no longer count towards your rating.
A question mark means the rating is still settling. It moves faster for your first 20 results.
Your ratings will show here as you solve puzzles and play rated games.

Square Chess keeps two ratings: one for puzzles and one for games against the computer. Both use the Elo formula that chess federations use: you gain more for beating a stronger opponent and lose more against a weaker one. Every computer level has a fixed rating, from 400 at level 1 to 2400 at level 10. These are estimates, so your game rating is a Square Chess rating and can differ from a FIDE or online rating. A game counts when you play the computer from the normal starting position, without the evaluation, hints or taking back moves. Resigning counts as a loss.
